report:
**Conclusion:** Your “no” is the best practical answer: coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) has **not been shown reliably enough to recommend it routinely** for statin-related muscle discomfort. It may help some people, but the overall evidence is small, mixed, and vulnerable to bias.

**Why the evidence is uncertain**

* The most rigorous placebo-controlled trial first used a statin/placebo crossover phase to identify people whose pain was genuinely statin-related. In the confirmed group, high-dose CoQ10 (600 mg/day) did **not** improve pain, muscle strength, or aerobic performance versus placebo. Importantly, only a minority of people who initially reported statin pain had symptoms that were reproducibly caused by the statin.  
  https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4298455/

* Some older, small randomized trials did report symptom improvements. Accordingly, a 2018 meta-analysis of 12 trials reported favorable pooled symptom results. But differences in who was enrolled, how “statin myalgia” and pain were measured, doses/formulations, and trial quality make a pooled positive result less decisive.  
  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30371340/

* Later reviews characterize trial evidence as conflicting/equivocal rather than establishing benefit.  
  https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9171566/  
  https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11845-021-02651-x

**Clinical implication:** Do not stop a statin or substitute CoQ10 without discussing it with the prescriber. Better-supported approaches include checking for other causes/interactions, temporarily stopping and rechallenging, lowering the dose, changing statins or dosing schedule, and adding evidence-based non-statin LDL-lowering treatment when needed. Urgent assessment is warranted for severe weakness, dark urine, or marked pain.
